name: Green New Deal
summary: The Green New Deal is a programme to answer climate change with a New Deal-scale mobilisation of public investment, tied to full employment, social rights and justice for the communities most harmed. Its founding texts, the 2008 Green New Deal Group report in Britain and the 2019 House resolution in the United States, call for a rapid shift to clean energy, a guaranteed job and health care for everyone and a just transition for workers. The British report adds re-regulating finance, capital controls and a crackdown on tax havens. It is a policy platform with no developed view on most of the questions a full politics must answer.

scope: The Green New Deal as set out by name in its two founding texts: the Green New Deal Group's 2008 report A Green New Deal and its 2009 follow-up (Britain), and the 2019 House resolution H.Res. 109 'Recognizing the duty of the Federal Government to create a Green New Deal' (United States), read with the scholars who define it (Stilwell, Pollin, Mastini, Kallis and Hickel). Where the two founding texts speak to a statement, the answer follows them; a position found in only one is cited to it. The European Green Deal, other countries' plans, and party versions such as the US Green Party's 'Ecosocialist Green New Deal' (which calls the Democrats' version too weak) are other subjects and are not used. Barbier's UN 'Global Green New Deal' and the Routledge Handbook could not be opened.

notes: Themes searched: economy, government, society, world, liberty, ecology, means, globalism, in the two founding texts and the scholarship above. The texts are policy platforms, so most statements on liberty, culture, religion, family, the state and war are null. The two founding texts come from different countries and years, so positions found in only one (capital controls, central banks, tax havens, climate finance for poor countries in the 2008 report; labor rights, Indigenous consent, health care in H.Res. 109) are cited to it alone. Not used: the US Green Party's Ecosocialist Green New Deal (saved in the library), which is a party's variant that rejects the Democratic version. Pollin's article could only be read as far as the free opening and Mastini et al. only as an abstract; both are cited only for what that text shows. Barbier's UN brief, the Routledge Handbook and Stilwell's journal article could not be opened (see notFound).
